title: From clusters back to real neurons
objective: Explain how transcriptomic subtypes connect to Cre lines and the lab's work.

steps.title: Closing the loop
steps.body: A transcriptomic subtype is only useful if you can *get at* it. The loop: sequencing proposes a marker → **[[RNAscope]]** confirms it in tissue → a **[[Cre]]** line (ideally intersectional, C3) built on that marker lets you label, record, or silence the subtype.

steps.prompt: Order the path from data to manipulation.
items: Single-cell RNA-seq proposes a subtype and marker
RNAscope confirms the marker in real neurons
A Cre (or Cre/Flp) line targets that marker
AAV delivers a tool (reporter, GCaMP, DREADD)
steps.explanation: Each step turns a cluster into a handle you can actually grab in an experiment.

steps.prompt: Why isn't a sequencing cluster, by itself, enough to study a subtype's function?
options: You still need a way to label and manipulate those cells in vivo
Clusters only count once a second dataset reproduces them
Function needs a protein readout, so run a western first
A marker gene's expression already tells you its function
steps.explanation: A cluster is a description. Testing function needs genetic access — a marker you can build a Cre line and viral tools around.

variants.setup: You have a cluster and its marker gene.
variants.prompt: What's still needed to test its function?
options: Genetic access — a Cre line and tools — to the cells
Just a larger single-cell dataset with more cells
Only RNAscope confirming the marker in the tissue
variants.reveal: You need a handle — a Cre line and viral tools — to manipulate the subtype.

steps.title: This is your project's backbone
steps.body: Finding pancreas-innervating sensory subtypes, confirming their markers, and building genetic access to silence them with a **[[DREADD]]** is this exact loop — transcriptome to tool. Track C has walked each piece; the capstone puts them together.

sources.citation: Usoskin D et al., 2015, Nat Neurosci
sources.note: Single-cell RNA-seq classification of DRG sensory neuron types.
